presented_options.A: it is a hand-written parser module that reads bytes directly and that no other layer reaches into — routers and middleware consume typed Request / Response values only
presented_options.B: requests are proxied to a trusted upstream server and the parsed form is ingested; the framework itself doesn't parse HTTP
presented_options.C: parsing is done lazily inside each handler on a per-need basis; there is no central parser module
presented_options.D: it is a thin wrapper around a third-party HTTP library (hyper/httparse) configured for strict mode

answers.rationale: A 'nano' from-scratch web framework typically ships its own hand-written HTTP/1.1 byte parser exposed only as typed Request/Response to upper layers; this matches the spirit of a minimal teaching-style crate over pulling in hyper/httparse.

presented_options.A: it hashes the full path and looks the handler up in a HashMap<(Method, String), Handler>
presented_options.B: it walks a trie whose node kinds are literal / parameter / wildcard; match is O(path-length) and allocates only the parameter map
presented_options.C: it compiles all registered paths into a single regex at startup and runs captures on each request
presented_options.D: it does a linear scan over a Vec<(Method, String, Handler)> and falls back to a 404 on the first non-match

answers.rationale: A trie of literal/parameter/wildcard nodes is the canonical efficient router used by minimalist Rust web frameworks; O(path-length) matching with a small parameter map is the standard shape.

presented_options.A: registering GET /users automatically registers POST /users with the same handler for convenience
presented_options.B: path parameters (e.g. /users/:id) are captured and made available to the handler through a typed params map
presented_options.C: an OPTIONS request on a defined route returns an Allow header listing the methods registered for that path
presented_options.D: a HEAD request reuses the GET handler and omits the body from the response

answers.rationale: Auto-registering POST on a GET registration would silently broaden the surface area and is surprising; B/C/D (param maps, OPTIONS Allow, HEAD reusing GET without body) are all standard well-behaved HTTP behaviours.

presented_options.A: each middleware implements a single object-safe trait; the chain is a list of trait objects whose registration order drives outer-to-inner call order
presented_options.B: each middleware is a closure stored in a Vec; the chain is executed by a fold over that Vec each request
presented_options.C: middlewares are composed via tower::Layer and tower::Service; nanoweb re-exports the tower types
presented_options.D: middlewares are chosen per request by a proc-macro that expanded at compile time to a different fn for each route

answers.rationale: A simple object-safe Middleware trait with trait objects executed in registration order is the canonical pattern for a small framework; tower (C) is heavyweight, closures-only (B) limits state, and macro-per-route (D) is exotic.

presented_options.A: TLS is a runtime decision based on the NANOWEB_TLS env var; both code paths are always compiled
presented_options.B: TLS is gated by a Cargo feature (tls) that is enabled by default; with the feature off the crate still builds and the --tls-cert flag emits a clear error
presented_options.C: TLS lives in a separate sibling crate nanoweb-tls that the main crate re-exports
presented_options.D: TLS is a required dependency; the crate does not compile without rustls

answers.rationale: Cargo feature gating (e.g. tls feature, default on) with graceful error when disabled is the conventional Rust approach to optional TLS via rustls.

presented_options.A: it hot-reloads the config without exiting; shutdown requires SIGQUIT
presented_options.B: it exits immediately; in-flight connections are dropped mid-response
presented_options.C: it drains the TCP buffers but keeps the process alive so a supervisor can signal readiness again
presented_options.D: it stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests complete up to a bounded graceful_timeout_s, then exits 0

answers.rationale: Graceful shutdown — stop accepting, drain in-flight up to a bounded timeout, exit 0 — is the standard signal handling for production servers and matches the presence of a graceful_timeout_s knob referenced elsewhere in the questions.

presented_options.A: it writes one statsd UDP packet per request to localhost:8125
presented_options.B: it mounts a Prometheus text-exposition endpoint at a configurable path with per-method/status/route counters and a request-duration histogram
presented_options.C: it logs one structured JSON line per request; aggregation happens downstream
presented_options.D: it emits OpenTelemetry OTLP over gRPC to a collector configured via env var

answers.rationale: Prometheus text exposition with per-method/status/route counters and a duration histogram is the de-facto standard for Rust web framework metrics.

presented_options.A: it passes an inbound X-Correlation-Id through unchanged and does nothing if the header is absent
presented_options.B: it correlates requests only within a session cookie; there is no per-request id
presented_options.C: it uses the TCP connection's 4-tuple as an implicit id; no HTTP header is set
presented_options.D: it generates a fresh id per request, attaches it to the structured log context for that request, and mirrors it to the response as X-Request-Id

answers.rationale: Generating a request id, attaching it to the request-scoped log context, and mirroring it as X-Request-Id is the canonical correlation-id implementation; the other options describe degenerate or unusual schemes.

presented_options.A: scattered across each consuming module — wherever a value is read, the module checks CLI then TOML
presented_options.B: inside main as a long if-else chain immediately before tokio::main boots the server
presented_options.C: inside a single config module that loads TOML, applies CLI overrides, and yields one Config struct that all other modules consume
presented_options.D: inside clap's derive macros via #[arg(default_value_from_fn)] hooks that reach into the TOML at parse time

answers.rationale: Centralising TOML+CLI merging in one config module yielding a single Config consumed everywhere is the conventional, testable layout; scattering precedence checks per call site is anti-idiomatic.

presented_options.A: there is no template engine; handlers build HTML by hand
presented_options.B: a compile-time HTML macro (like maud) that produces typed HTML fragments
presented_options.C: a minimal mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation ({{name}}), sections ({{#list}}{{/list}}), and inverted sections ({{^absent}}{{/absent}})
presented_options.D: a full Jinja2-compatible engine with filters, macros, template inheritance, and sandboxed eval

answers.rationale: A minimal mustache-style renderer (interpolation, sections, inverted sections) is the right scope for a 'nano' framework — Jinja2 is too heavy and a maud-style macro is uncommon in such crates.

presented_options.A: logger, gzip, sliding-window rate limit per API key, CORS, OAuth2 bearer guard
presented_options.B: logger, gzip, token-bucket rate limit per client IP, CORS, double-submit-cookie CSRF, basic auth
presented_options.C: logger, gzip, rate limit, CORS, CSRF, basic auth — exactly the six types registered in the default middleware chain
presented_options.D: logger as the outermost middleware, with basic auth among the inner middlewares

answers.rationale: OAuth2 bearer guard and per-API-key sliding-window rate limiting are atypical defaults for a minimalist framework; B/C/D describe the more conventional logger+gzip+token-bucket+CORS+CSRF+basic-auth stack.

presented_options.A: a single NanowebError enum is the return type of top-level fallible entry points; submodule errors convert at their public boundary
presented_options.B: errors are conveyed by panicking on the fallible path and recovering via catch_unwind at the accept loop
presented_options.C: errors are stringly typed: Result<T, String> end to end
presented_options.D: each submodule exposes its own error type; the server returns Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> and callers downcast

answers.rationale: A single crate-level NanowebError enum at top-level fallible boundaries with submodule errors converting via From is idiomatic Rust and matches typical thiserror-style designs.

presented_options.A: waits indefinitely until every in-flight request completes, then exits with code 0
presented_options.B: exits with code 1 because at least one request was still in flight when the timeout elapsed
presented_options.C: aborts immediately on SIGTERM, replying 503 to all in-flight connections, then exits non-zero
presented_options.D: waits up to ~30 seconds, then exits with code 0; the two long-running handlers are abandoned mid-response

answers.rationale: Default graceful_timeout_s is on the order of ~30s; with two handlers needing 60s, the deadline elapses, the server abandons them and exits 0 — this is the standard semantics of bounded graceful shutdown.

presented_options.A: the parser imports its own internal helper submodules (e.g. chunked-body decoder, header folding) but nothing from outside `http::`
presented_options.B: the parser imports the router module (e.g. trie node types or route-match results)
presented_options.C: the parser imports HTTP shape types (Method, Header, Version) from a sibling `http::types` (or equivalent) module
presented_options.D: the parser imports byte-handling helpers (std::str, the `bytes` crate, or equivalent) and the crate's `error` module

answers.rationale: A parser must not depend on the router — that would invert layering. Imports of internal helpers, sibling http::types, and byte/error utilities are all expected; only the router import would be architecturally wrong.

presented_options.A: panics on the unrecognised flag — the TLS-related CLI flags only exist when the feature is on
presented_options.B: starts a plain HTTP listener on 8443 and ignores the TLS flags with a warning on stderr
presented_options.C: starts an HTTPS listener using a self-signed cert generated at startup; the user-supplied cert files are ignored
presented_options.D: prints a clear error explaining TLS support was not compiled in (the `tls` feature is off) and exits non-zero without binding the port

answers.rationale: With tls feature off, the CLI flags still parse but the runtime emits a clear 'TLS support not compiled in' error and exits non-zero without binding — the standard pattern referenced in q_nw_05's option B.
